prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with B029 (circuit QED) first, but after reading the other seven ballots I move B030 to the head of my configuration. The optical lattice clock is a clean case of an original idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which cancels light shifts) followed by decisive realization (Ye's record accuracy and stability, many-body clock physics and comparison technology). It has been reproduced independently in several national laboratories, has reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, and already supports tests of relativity, searches for varying constants and relativistic geodesy. The two-person credit is unusually clean for a modern instrument-driven discovery. Six of eight members ranked it in their top three, and three placed it first, and that spread across atomic physics, particle theory, computation and condensed matter is more informative than my own enthusiasm for any single candidate.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is partial overlap with earlier metrology prizes (the 2005 award for the frequency comb and the 2012 award for control of single trapped ions), which some members may read as a prior payment on the same field. Other groups (single-ion clock groups, and lattice-clock groups outside the credited names such as Lemonde's) contributed to performance, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the practical culmination is still pending. I have also not independently verified every uncertainty record claimed for the best clocks, and my own reading of the clock literature is that of an outsider to atomic metrology.

responses.point: Ranks B030 first as a conceptual invention (magic-wavelength proposal) plus realization, with Katori and Ye as a clean pair, but notes boundary questions with earlier frequency-metrology prizes and that the redefinition of the second is pending.
responses.response: I agree on the pair and on maturity, and I think the boundary question is answerable: the 2005 and 2012 prizes recognised the comb and single-ion quantum control, whereas the lattice clock's distinctive step is interrogating many neutral atoms in a trap where the light shift is engineered away. I would not make the prize contingent on the redefinition of the second, since the discovery is already validated by independent clocks agreeing at the 1e-18 level. I would, however, keep the citation to the invention and realization rather than the redefinition, so we do not claim something that has not happened.

responses.point: Ranks B030 first and B029 fourth. She flags that Wallraff is missing from the B029 credit, that its closeness to the 2025 award may lower its priority, and that overlapping topological entries B058 and B032 differ in support.
responses.response: I accept her B029 criticisms, and they changed my own ranking. As a Chalmers professor working in this field I have an obvious bias toward circuit QED, and the supplied trio omits Wallraff, who carried out the 2004 strong-coupling experiment. That is a real credit gap, not a technicality. I also agree that the timing is uncomfortable so soon after 2025. Where I would qualify her view is on B030: she treats the prior frequency-metrology awards as a risk that some members may hold, and I think the committee should state plainly why lattice clocks are a separate achievement rather than leave it implicit.

responses.point: Ranks IceCube (B020) first as a genuine discovery that opened a new observational window, with Halzen and Karle central and a third place open for Spiering. He also puts Higgs (B017) second.
responses.response: I take the scientific merit of B020 seriously, and I ranked it sixth rather than dismissing it. My reservations are about attribution and about how complete the picture is: the diffuse flux is secure, but the origin of most of it is unresolved, and he himself leaves the third name open, which tells me the credit is not settled among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA lineage. B030 has a cleaner two-name allocation and a more fully realised payoff. If the committee does prefer B020 I would argue for the three-name version, but I do not think the opening support, which is only two first places and three ranked ballots, shows it is stronger than B030.

responses.point: Ranks Car and Parrinello (B022) first because the 1985 paper has exactly two authors, the method is overdue after four decades, and its home in a physics prize rather than chemistry is a judgement call.
responses.response: The two-author clarity of B022 is a real merit, and I do not dismiss the methodological impact. Where I differ is on the Nobel criteria: I would want the committee to be satisfied that a computational method is a discovery or invention in physics, and the ballot support (only two members ranked it) suggests most colleagues are not yet satisfied. I rank it below B030 and have left it out of my alternatives, but I would not oppose its being weighed in the next round if the physics-versus-chemistry question is answered.

uncertainties: How the committee weighs the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes against a lattice-clock award.
Whether other lattice-clock groups outside the credited pair have credit claims strong enough to alter the two-name configuration.
Whether the planned redefinition of the second should be mentioned in the citation or left out until it occurs.
For my alternatives B029 and B004: the Wallraff gap and Esslinger/Jaksch credit respectively are unresolved within three names.
statement.conflict_note: I am a professor at Chalmers and director of WACQT, with documented ties to Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum. Circuit QED (B029) is my own research area and Chalmers hosted researchers connected to the 2025 prize, so I should be recused from weighing B029, and I have treated it only as an alternative. No specific personal or institutional connection to the B030 (Katori, Ye) or B004 candidates is apparent from my profile.
